rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After prohibitions against fornication and unjust killing, which prevent destruction of human life, the verse turns to property, the most valuable thing after life, and singles out vulnerable orphans for protection.
rows.anchor: وأما القتل فهو عبارة عن إعدام الناس بعد دخولهم في الوجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of protecting an orphan's property is to manage it in a way that grows and increases it.
rows.anchor: إلا بالتصرف الذي ينميه ويكثره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation permits a needy guardian to eat from the orphan's property while caring for it; Razi links this to the allowance in 4:6.
rows.anchor: المراد هو أن تأكل معه إذا احتجت إليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Mujahid transmits Ibn Abbas's rule: a needy guardian may eat reasonably and repay if later able; if never able, nothing is owed.
rows.anchor: إذا احتاج أكل بالمعروف فإذا أيسر قضاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guardianship lasts until the orphan reaches puberty and can manage property with sound judgment; if physical puberty comes without full rational capacity, guardianship continues.
rows.anchor: فأما إذا بلغ غير كامل العقل لم تزل الولاية عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A covenant is any agreement made to establish and confirm a matter; the command covers sales, partnerships, oaths, vows, settlements, and marriage.
rows.anchor: كل عقد تقدم لأجل توثيق الأمر وتوكيده فهو عهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every agreement between two people must be fulfilled unless separate evidence shows it is not binding; consensual sales and partnerships therefore default to validity.
rows.anchor: كل عقد وعهد جرى بين إنسانين فإنه يجب عليهما الوفاء

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is cited to say that a Muslim's property is lawful to take only with the owner's willing consent.
rows.anchor: لا يحل مال امرىء مسلم إلا عن طيبة من نفسه

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is cited on exchange between different commodity classes: trade as desired provided delivery is hand to hand.
rows.anchor: إذا اختلف الجنسان فبيعوا كيف شئتم يدا بيد

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is cited to give a buyer who purchased an unseen item the option to accept or reject it upon seeing it.
rows.anchor: من اشترى شيئا لم يره فهو بالخيار إذا رآه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These proofs establish a general presumption of validity and binding force for transactions; specific textual evidence overrides the general rule, while Razi rejects using analogy to restrict it.
rows.anchor: إن وجدنا نصا أخص من هذه النصوص يدل على البطلان والفساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading makes the covenant-holder the person questioned, with an omitted possessive; Razi compares this ellipsis to asking a town, meaning its residents.
rows.anchor: أن يراد صاحب العهد كان مسؤلا فحذف المضاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading takes the covenant itself as something demanded: the contracting party is required not to neglect it but to fulfill it.
rows.anchor: العهد كان مسؤلا أي مطلوبا يطلب من المعاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading rhetorically addresses the covenant to reproach the breaker, as scripture addresses the buried girl or Jesus while rebuking others.
rows.anchor: أن يكون هذا تخييلا كأنه يقال للعهد لم نكثت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to give full measure is reinforced by the threat against sellers who take full measure from others but give them less.
rows.anchor: والمقصود منه إتمام الكيل وذكر الوعيد الشديد في نقصانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next command concerns full weight, parallel to commands to weigh fairly and not deprive people of their goods.
rows.anchor: فالآية المتقدمة في إتمام الكيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even a small shortfall draws a severe threat because everyone depends on exchange, some fail to guard their property, and cheating steals even a tiny due amount from its owner.
rows.anchor: فالشارع بالغ في المنع من التطفيف والنقصان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qistas means a balance, conventionally a larger steelyard; some call the word Roman or Syriac, but Razi prefers Arabic derivation from qist, fairness and balance.
rows.anchor: والأصح أنه لغة العرب وهو مأخوذ من القسط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both pronunciations of qistas, with kasra or damma on qaf, are accepted; Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read kasra, and the others damma.
rows.anchor: وأجمعوا على جواز اللغتين فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Full measure is better than slight cheating because it avoids disgrace in this life and punishment in the next; ta'wil means the eventual outcome, as in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: والتأويل ما يؤل إليه الأمر كما قال في موضع آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Honest dealing earns public trust, affection, and wealth quickly in this world; in the next it brings reward and escape from punishment.
rows.anchor: عول الناس عليه ومالت القلوب إليه وحصل له الاستغناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qafa means to follow someone's trace: the poetic rhyme follows its line, trackers follow footprints, and qafa names the back as what follows the body; the verse broadly forbids following or judging by anything unknown, in word or deed.
rows.anchor: قفوت أثر فلان أقفو قفوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation rebukes polytheists for inherited beliefs about God and prophethood founded on desire rather than evidence.
rows.anchor: المراد نهي المشركين عن المذاهب التي كانوا يعتقدونها

rows.speaker: محمد بن الحنفية
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya explains the prohibition as a ban on giving false testimony.
rows.anchor: نقل عن محمد بن الحنفية أن المراد منه شهادة الزور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says testimony must be limited to what one's eyes saw, ears heard, and heart understood.
rows.anchor: لا تشهد إلا بما رأته عيناك وسمعته أذناك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation forbids slandering chaste men and women with lies, a practice Arabs commonly used and exaggerated in invective.
rows.anchor: النهي عن القذف ورمي المحصنين والمحصنات بالأكاذيب

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains it as a ban on lying: do not claim to have heard, seen, or known what you have not.
rows.anchor: لا تقل سمعت ولم تسمع ورأيت ولم تر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another meaning is slander or backbiting: qafw derives from the nape, as speech made behind someone's back that he dislikes.
rows.anchor: أن القفو هو البهت وأصله من القفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report warns that whoever falsely attributes something to a Muslim will be confined by God in radghat al-khabal; Razi gives no grading or source authority.
rows.anchor: من قفا مسلما بما ليس فيه حبسه الله في ردغة الخبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the wording is general, it encompasses all these applications rather than being restricted to one by imitation.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن اللفظ عام يتناول الكل فلا معنى للتقليد

rows.speaker: نفاة القياس
rows.claim: Those who reject analogy argue that it yields probability rather than knowledge, so ruling by analogy in religion is prohibited by this verse.
rows.anchor: القياس لا يفيد إلا الظن والظن مغاير للعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that probability is accepted by consensus in many religious cases: fatwas, testimony, finding the qibla, compensation estimates, medicine, identifying slaughter, appointing arbiters, Muslim status, and ordinary worldly decisions.
rows.anchor: الحكم في الدين بمجرد الظن جائز بإجماع الأمة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is cited for judging by outward appearances while leaving inner realities to God, supporting reliance on probability.
rows.anchor: قال عليه السلام : ( نحن نحكم بالظاهر والله يتولى السرائر )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that probability may be called knowledge, citing the command to test believing emigrant women and accept their professed faith; he says the reading is that they profess belief.
rows.anchor: والجواب الثاني : أن الظن قد يسمى بالعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further defense says decisive proof makes the analogical ruling certain even if probability lies on the route to it.
rows.anchor: والجواب الثالث : أن الدليل القاطع لما دل على وجوب العمل بالقياس

rows.speaker: نفاة القياس
rows.claim: Analogy's opponents reply that accepted probabilistic cases are necessary individual judgments that cannot all be textually specified, whereas analogical rulings are few, general rules that could have been stated explicitly.
rows.anchor: أجاب نفاة القياس عن السؤال الأول فقالوا : قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects equating probability with knowledge: one can distinguish the probable from the known, and 6:148 contrasts conjecture with knowledge; in 60:10, knowledge means recognizing a woman's profession of faith.
rows.anchor: وأما الجواب الثاني : وهو قولهم الظن قد يسمى علما فنقول : هذا باطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that analogy has decisive proof is weak: rationally, a lawgiver could forbid it, and no transmitted proof is both mass-transmitted and unambiguous; disagreement shows no such proof exists.
rows.anchor: وأما الجواب الثالث : فهو أيضا ضعيف ، لأن ذلك الكلام إنما يتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The strongest reply is that using this verse against probability relies on a specified general text and so yields only probability; if probability is forbidden, the argument defeats itself.
rows.anchor: فلو دلت هذه الآية على أن التمسك بالظن غير جائز لدلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A response says the binding force of Qur'anic verses is known by widespread transmission; Razi notes that the binding force of a specified general text is not itself known that way.
rows.anchor: وللمجيب أن يجيب فيقول : نعلم بالتواتر الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hearing and sight represent knowledge received through the senses, while the heart represents rational knowledge, both intuitive and acquired.
rows.anchor: فإن الإنسان إذا سمع شيئا ورآه فإنه يرويه ويخبر عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says the person who owns the faculties is questioned, since organs cannot understand; he is asked why he listened, looked, or intended what was forbidden.
rows.anchor: أن المراد أن صاحب السمع والبصر والفؤاد هو المسؤول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation says people are questioned about how they used every faculty, which is the soul's instrument: good use merits reward and sinful use punishment.
rows.anchor: أن أولئك الأقوام كلهم مسؤولون عن السمع والبصر والفؤاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation takes the organs themselves as witnesses; since 24:24 says body parts testify, God may create life, intellect, and speech in them and question them.
rows.anchor: أنه ثبت بالقرآن أنه تعالى يخلق الحياة في الأعضاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marah is intense joy; here it means walking in a manner that displays pride and grandeur. Al-Zajjaj glosses it as strutting arrogantly, parallel to humble walking and measured gait.
rows.anchor: والمراد من الآية النهي عن أن يمشي الإنسان مشيا يدل على الكبرياء

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says reading marahan with kasra would be better.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش : ولو قرى : { مرحا } بالكسر كان أحسن

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj allows marahan as a verbal noun or marahan as an active participle, preferring the verbal noun because it emphasizes the act.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : مرحا مصدر ومرحا اسم الفاعل وكلاهما جائز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of not penetrating earth or reaching mountains is that the proud walker can neither pierce downward nor climb to the peaks, proving human weakness.
rows.anchor: حال الانخفاض لا تقدر على خرق الأرض ونقبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says earth lies below and mountains above, enclosing humanity among inert matter; a weak, confined creature should be humble rather than act powerful.
rows.anchor: فأنت محاط بك من فوقك وتحتك بنوعين من الجماد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan supports the genitive reading si'ihi: since the passage contains commands as well as prohibitions, only its evil acts are detestable, not everything mentioned.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : إنه تعالى ذكر قبل هذا أشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority's genitive construction means the evil among the previously listed acts is detested, avoiding the claim that all of them are bad and detestable.
rows.anchor: أما إذا قرأناه بصيغة الإضافة كان المعنى أن سيىء تلك الأقسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafi, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read the accusative si'atan; one parsing ends the preceding statement at 17:35 and takes all later prohibitions as the referent of 'all that.'
rows.anchor: والمراد هذه الأشياء الأخيرة التي نهى الله عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second accusative-reading interpretation takes 'all that' to mean everything God prohibited earlier.
rows.anchor: أي كل ما نهى الله عنه فيما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To construe the accusative reading with makruhan, one may supply 'and was detestable,' or treat si'ah like a noun such as sin whose grammatical gender no longer controls agreement.
rows.anchor: الأول : التقدير : كل ذلك كان سيئة وكان مكروها

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf treats si'ah as a noun like sin or transgression, so its feminine form can be predicated of masculine acts.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) : السيئة في حكم الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other repairs for the accusative reading are to reverse the order to 'detestable and evil,' or match the feminine word to its masculine meaning, sin.
rows.anchor: الثالث : فيه تقديم وتأخير ، والتقدير : كل ذلك كان مكروها

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi argues that because God detests these deeds, they are not His will and therefore cannot be His creation, since created deeds would be willed by Him.
rows.anchor: دلت هذه الآية على أن هذه الأعمال مكروهة عند الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that makruhan means forbidden; although this repeats the preceding idea, repetition for emphasis is acceptable.
rows.anchor: والجواب : أن المراد من المكروه المنهي عنه ولا بأس بالتكرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the objection that God could dislike an act yet will its occurrence, Razi says this passage warns against the deeds, so describing God as disliking their occurrence would not suit the context.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى إنما ذكر هذه الآية في معرض الزجر عن هذه الأفعال

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi infers from the verse that God is characterized both by willing and by aversion.
rows.anchor: دلت هذه الآية على أنه تعالى كما أنه موصوف بكونه مريدا

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Razi's school interprets divine aversion as either prohibition or willing that the deed not occur.
rows.anchor: الكراهية في حقه تعالى محمولة إما على النهي أو على إرادة العدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi counts twenty-five duties in the passage, combining commands and prohibitions, and frames the list between prohibitions of associating another deity.
rows.anchor: فهذه خمسة وعشرون نوعا من التكاليف بعضها أوامر وبعضها نواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The duties are wisdom because they center on monotheism, virtuous worship, and turning toward the afterlife, which reason and innate nature recognize as the Lord's religion.
rows.anchor: حاصلها يرجع إلى الأمر بالتوحيد وأنواع الطاعات والخيرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These commands are wisdom because they are binding across religions and cannot be abrogated, so they are definitive principles.
rows.anchor: شرائع واجبة الرعاية في جميع الأديان والملل ولا تقبل النسخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wisdom is knowing truth for its own sake and knowing good in order to practice it: monotheism teaches the first and the other duties teach the second.
rows.anchor: الحكمة عبارة عن معرفة الحق لذاته والخير لأجل العمل به

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says these commands appeared on Moses' tablets, whose contents are described in 7:145.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس : أن هذه الآيات كانت في ألواح موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening and closing the duties with monotheism teaches that every act, utterance, thought, and remembrance should begin and end with it; all duties aim at knowing and immersing oneself in tawhid.
rows.anchor: أول كل عمل وقول وفكر وذكر يجب أن يكون ذكر التوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first warning describes shirk's worldly blame and abandonment; the final warning describes its afterlife blame and expulsion. Blame first identifies the deed as bad, then reproaches its motive; abandonment means lack of aid, expulsion means humiliation.
rows.anchor: أما الفرق بين المذموم وبين الملوم ، فهو أن كونه مذموما معناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pagans deemed sons superior and daughters inferior, yet claimed sons for themselves despite their weakness and daughters for God despite His perfection, exposing the claim's absurdity.
rows.anchor: فأشرف القسمين البنون ، وأخسهما البنات

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda glosses asfakum as 'singled you out' or favored you.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة في قوله : { أفأصفاكم } أفخصكم

rows.speaker: المفضل
rows.claim: Al-Mufaddal glosses asfakum as 'gave exclusively' or selected for you.
rows.anchor: وقال المفضل : أخلصكم . قال النحويون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative hamza rebukes a manifestly false belief, whose answer can only expose its adherents to greater shame.
rows.anchor: هذه الهمزة همزة تدل على الإنكار على صيغة السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God a father implies composition from parts, contradicting His being pre-eternal and necessary in Himself.
rows.anchor: إثبات الولد يقتضي كونه تعالى مركبا من الأجزاء والأبعاض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim is also a grave error because it assigns the better category to humans and the inferior category to God.
rows.anchor: جعلتم أشرف القسمين لأنفسكم وأخس القسمين لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasrif literally turns something from one direction to another; it came to mean clarification because explaining a point shifts among kinds and examples. Its object is omitted, with one reading supplying varied parables in the Quran.
rows.anchor: ثم جعل لفظ التصريف كناية عن التبيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading treats fi as extra, as in 46:15, so the phrase means that God varied the Quran's explanations.
rows.anchor: وثانيها : أن تكون لفظة ( في ) زائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers vocalize li-yadhdhakkaru as 'so they may remember/reflect,' assimilating the t into the nearby dh; Hamza and al-Kisa'i read li-yadhkuru.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور { ليذكروا } بفتح الذال والكاف وتشديدهما

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi says reflection is more apt than recollection after forgetting; for the other reading, dhikr may mean contemplation, as in 2:63, or oral remembrance that affects the heart.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي : والتذكر ههنا أشبه من الذكر

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba'i argues that varying proofs shows God intended people to understand and believe, supporting the view that God acts for wise purposes and wanted faith from everyone.
rows.anchor: يدل على أنه تعالى أراد الإيمان من الكل سواء آمنوا أو كفروا

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Asamm compares the unbelievers to frightened animals: exposure to the truth only makes them flee farther from it.
rows.anchor: قال الأصم : شبههم بالدواب النافرة

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Razi's theological school argues that God did not intend faith from unbelievers: knowing the Quran's varied proofs increase their aversion, a wise agent seeking belief would avoid that effect.
rows.anchor: علمنا أنه ما أراد الإيمان منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading of the hypothetical about other gods invokes mutual prevention: if multiple gods existed, they would overpower one another, the argument from mutual hindrance also given at 21:22.
rows.anchor: وحاصله يرجع إلى دليل التمانع وقد شرحناه في سورة الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading addresses idolaters who say they worship idols to draw near to God: if the idols were truly intermediaries, they would seek their own access and higher rank with Him.
rows.anchor: فقال الله لو كانت هذه الأصنام كما تقولون من أنها تقربكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings of the pronouns differ: Ibn Kathir reads all three in third person; Hamza and al-Kisa'i use second person throughout; Nafi, Ibn Amir, and Abu Bakr vary them; Hafs reads the first two third person and the last second person; Abu Amr the first and last second person, middle third.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير كما يقولون وعما يقولون ويسبح بالياء في هذه الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subhanahu means declaring God free of what does not befit Him; His exaltation is not spatial elevation, since transcendence over partners and defects cannot mean height in a place or direction.
rows.anchor: وظاهر أن المراد من هذا التعالي ليس هو التعالي في المكان والجهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse uses the verbal noun uluwwan where a verbal noun of ta'ali might be expected, parallel to 71:17.
rows.anchor: وكان يجب أن يقال تعالى تعاليا كبيرا إلا أن نظيره قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The epithet 'great' fits because God's nature and attributes are utterly incompatible with consort, child, partners, opposites, and equals: necessary versus possible, eternal versus originated, and self-sufficient versus needy.
rows.anchor: المنافاة بين الواجب / لذاته والممكن لذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Living, accountable beings glorify God verbally and by displaying His unity and perfection; animals and inanimate objects can only glorify through the latter evidence, since speech-based praise requires understanding and life.
rows.anchor: فأما الذي لا يكون مكلفا مثل البهائم ، ومن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allowing inert matter to know and speak would undermine the proof that knowledge and power entail life, contrary to the necessary truth that what is not alive cannot know, act, or speak; he says recognized scholars uphold this.
rows.anchor: أن من ليس بحي لم يكن عالما قادرا متكلما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some argue that animals, plants, and inert objects literally praise God: because people cannot understand their praise, it must be distinct from their evident testimony to divine power and wisdom.
rows.anchor: إن الجمادات وأنواع النبات والحيوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Answering this, Razi says every indivisible part of an apple, and each contingent feature assigned to it, independently testifies to a wise, powerful creator; their uncounted parts and features explain why people do not comprehend this praise.
rows.anchor: دليل تام على وجود الإله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second answer is that polytheists professed a creator but did not contemplate the signs around them, so they failed to grasp the world's testimony to God.
rows.anchor: كانوا يقرون بألسنتهم بإثبات إله العالم إلا أنهم ما كانوا يتفكرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third answer is that they did not recognize God's full power, doubted resurrection, and missed the proof from mutual hindrance; the heavens and earth attest to that proof.
rows.anchor: استبعدوا كونه تعالى قادرا على الحشر والنشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More broadly, they overlooked most proofs of divine unity, justice, prophecy, and resurrection; calling this ignorance a grave fault and pairing it with God's forbearance and forgiveness suits failure to recognize evidence, not inaudible verbal praise.
rows.anchor: ذكر الحليم والغفور ههنا يدل على أن كونهم بحيث لا يفقهون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal-praise view is inconsistent: its advocates say slaughter stops an animal's praise and breaking stops a branch's, although being inanimate supposedly does not prevent praise.
rows.anchor: صار ذبح الحيوان مانعا له من التسبيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the verse includes both rational beings who literally say 'glory be to God' and inanimate things whose state signifies God's transcendence, the same verb would be literal and metaphorical at once, which legal theory rejects; Razi therefore takes it metaphorically for inanimate things.
rows.anchor: فالأولى أن يحمل هذا التسبيح على الوجه المجازي في حق الجمادات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One occasion report says men from Qusay's descendants stood on both sides of the Prophet while he recited, clapping, whistling, and mixing in poetry to disturb him.
rows.anchor: يصفقون ويصفرون ويخلطون عليه بالأشعار

rows.speaker: أسماء
rows.claim: Asma reports that Abu Lahab's wife approached Abu Bakr and the Prophet with a stone, threatening him; after he recited the verse she could not see him, and Abu Bakr denied that he had satirized her.
rows.anchor: وعن أسماء أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم كان جالسا ومعه أبو بكر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that Abu Sufyan, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu Jahl, Abu Lahab, and Huwaytib each made dismissive comments as they listened; the passage was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: أن أبا سفيان والنضر بن الحرث وأبا جهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before reciting, the Prophet read three verses—18:57, 16:108, and 45:23—and God protected him from the polytheists' sight through their blessing, the hidden barrier of this verse.
rows.anchor: قرأ قبلها ثلاثة آيات وهي قوله في سورة الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi's preferred answer is that God creates an unseen barrier in the unbelievers' eyes; it supports his school's view that healthy senses and a present object need not result in perception if God creates an impediment.
rows.anchor: ذلك الحجاب حجاب يخلقه الله تعالى في عيونهم بحيث يمنعهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second answer treats mastur as 'possessing a covering,' by analogy with words meaning possessed of milk, dates, moisture, terror, or flirtation.
rows.anchor: أن يقال مستورا معناه ذو ستر

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says mastur means satir, 'covering'; an active sense can use the passive form, as in mash'um and maymun.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش : المستور ههنا بمعنى الساتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second overall interpretation takes the veil as the seal or innate disposition on their hearts that blocks insight into the Quran's subtleties, benefits, and beauties.
rows.anchor: أن معنى الحجاب الطبع الذي على قلوبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akinna is the plural of kinnan, a covering such as an arrow quiver; the phrase means 'so that they do not understand,' and waqran is a heaviness in their ears.
rows.anchor: والأكنة جمع كنان وهو ما ستر الشيء مثل كنان النبل

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Razi's theological school reads the verse as God preventing unbelievers from believing and from hearing the Quran's secrets and fine meanings, despite their ordinary intelligence and hearing.
rows.anchor: فعلمنا أن المراد منعهم عن الإيمان ومنعهم عن سماع القرآن

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba'i says hostile people searched for the Prophet's lodging at night to harm him and tracked his recitation; God protected him with a barrier and distracted them from the Quran, not by literally covering hearts or weighing ears.
rows.anchor: كانوا يطلبون موضعه في الليالي لينتهوا إليه ويؤذونه

rows.speaker: الكعبي
rows.claim: Al-Ka'bi says their stubborn refusal made it as though a barrier separated them from Muhammad's proofs; God is said to have caused it because He left them to themselves instead of stopping their turning away.
rows.anchor: لشدة امتناعهم عن قبول دلائل محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم صاروا

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal says God created the barrier by abandoning them, withholding the subtle graces that would incline them toward faith.
rows.anchor: إنه تعالى لما خذلهم بمعنى أنه لم يفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says these alternative explanations and objections were already covered in his commentary on al-An'am, so he will not repeat that discussion.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن هذه الوجوه مع كلمات أخرى ذكرناها في سورة الأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the recited passage lacks explicit mention of God, they remain stunned and understand nothing; when it mentions God and condemns shirk, they turn away and leave.
rows.anchor: إذا سمعوا من القرآن ما ليس فيه ذكر الله تعالى بقوا مبهوتين

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj gives two parses of nufuran: a verbal noun meaning they turned away in flight, or a plural of nafir, 'one who flees,' like other plural participles.
rows.anchor: المصدر والمعنى ولوا نافرين نفورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows the manner in which they listen: mockingly and in denial. Bihi is circumstantial, idh specifies the time governed by 'knows,' and idh yaqulu is an apposition to their private conference.
rows.anchor: أي نحن أعلم بالوجه الذي يستمعون به وهو الهزؤ والتكذيب

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Commentators report that Muhammad asked Ali to prepare food for Quraysh notables, recited the Quran, and invited them to monotheism; they refused and privately called him a sorcerer or bewitched, which God revealed to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: أمر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عليا أن يتخذ طعاما ويدعو إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse quotes their private accusation that the audience is following only a bewitched man; Razi begins to question how they could say this when they had not followed the Prophet.
rows.anchor: فإن قيل : إنهم لم يتبعوا رسول الله فكيف يصح أن يقولوا
